models.description: Predicts per-atom MBIS (Minimal Basis Iterative Stockholder) partial charges via a graph-convolutional electronegativity-equalization model (jthorton/nagl-mbis, built on OpenFF's NAGL). Different architecture from the Chemprop models above -- see notes.
models.notes: This is jthorton/nagl-mbis's own pretrained checkpoint (nagl-v1-mbis-dipole.ckpt), not something trained as part of this project -- reused, not created. Despite the '-dipole' filename, inspected directly and confirmed single-readout (mbis-charges only). Genuinely different architecture from every other model in this registry: node-only GraphSAGE convolution (no bond features enter the convolution at all, confirmed from real NAGL/nagl-mbis source), 19-dim atom features (element/connectivity/ring-size), and a closed-form electronegativity-equalization postprocess that analytically guarantees predicted charges sum to the molecule's total formal charge -- not a plain regression head. Requires explicit hydrogens as real graph nodes (added internally, not something you need to draw) -- this app's other models work directly on the heavy-atom skeleton. VALIDATION: bit-exact confirmed against the real reference implementation. A conda env with a working DGL + naglmbis install was later found on the dev machine, making it possible to run jthorton/nagl-mbis's actual MBISGraphModel.compute_properties() (real DGL SAGEConv, not a reimplementation) directly and diff its output against this project's JS port across 28 molecules -- every element in the trained vocabulary, charged species ([NH4+], carboxylate anion), fused rings, ring sizes 3-6, and degree 1-4 edge cases. Max per-atom charge discrepancy was ~2e-7 (float32 rounding noise), and this same diffing process is what surfaced the '-dipole' checkpoint identity fact above (confirmed by comparing raw state_dict tensors, not assumed).

models.notes: Trained end-to-end this session (data fetch -> RDKit validation -> chemprop train -> convert -> JS validation), not a reused/pre-existing checkpoint. JS port cross-validated against all 679 real held-out test-set predictions (not just a hand-picked sanity set), by running this app's actual chemprop-model.js/graph-builder.js/chemprop-features.js/dmpnn.js pipeline headlessly in Node (RDKit.js WASM via @rdkit/rdkit) rather than eyeballing a few molecules in the browser: 675/679 (99.4%) match Chemprop's own Python predictions to <1e-3, mean abs error 0.0018 log units (negligible next to the model's own 0.576 test MAE). This surfaced and fixed one real, previously-undetected bug in chemprop-features.js's guessHybridization(): cumulated double bonds on a single atom (isocyanate/isothiocyanate N=C=O / N=C=S, CS2's S=C=S, allene-type centers) were classified as ordinary sp2 carbonyl-style, when they're actually SP (two independent pi systems only fit a linear/sp center) -- before the fix, 14/679 molecules (2.1%) had this discrepancy, several with >0.4 log-unit error; after, only 4/679 (0.6%) remain, all under 0.5 log units and concentrated in chiral-center/E-Z-adjacent structures already within this pipeline's documented known-approximation scope (see CHEMPROP_INTEGRATION.md). Fixed in chemprop-features.js so it applies to every model using this pipeline, not just this one -- worth spot-checking the other regression models' test sets for isocyanates/thiocyanates/CS2-like fragments if any exist, since none of their prior validations would have exercised this code path.

models.displayName: Carbon acid pKa, C-H bonds (per atom)
models.description: Predicts the pKa of C-H bonds (deprotonation to a stabilized carbanion) per candidate carbon site -- a from-scratch LightGBM/DART regressor trained on jensengroup/pKalculator's published training data (Ree et al., 'pKalculator: A pKa predictor for C-H bonds', ChemRxiv 2024, 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-56h5h), reproducing their graph-charge-shell descriptor construction but using this app's own NAGL-MBIS partial charges instead of the original method's CM5/GFN1-xTB charges (CM5 needs a real xtb binary subprocess, which has no WASM build and cannot run client-side). See notes for the honest accuracy comparison against the original CM5-based model.

dataset.name: pKalculator training set (Ree et al. 2024)
dataset.size: 759 of 775 molecules (16 dropped: contain Se, Si, or I, outside NAGL-MBIS's trained element vocabulary), 3675 of 4132 candidate C-H sites (outlier=True rows and sites with null/inf QM-derived targets dropped), same molecule-level train(620)/test(155) split the paper itself defines
dataset.splitStrategy: paper-defined molecule-level train/test split (dataset_full.pkl's own train_test column) -- not re-split here

hyperparameters.architecture: LightGBM, DART boosting, 1439 trees (round count picked from a fold1 train/val curve, then retrained on the full official train split)
hyperparameters.descriptor: graph charge shell (n_shells=6, CIP-priority + charge tiebreak sort), 1457 features, built from NAGL-MBIS charges over the full heavy+explicit-H atom graph
hyperparameters.lightgbmParams: num_leaves=868, max_depth=8, learning_rate=0.168, min_data_in_leaf=52, feature_fraction=0.548, bagging_fraction=0.756, bagging_freq=5, max_bin=476, lambda_l1=0.0107, lambda_l2=6.07e-06 -- reused directly from the original paper's own Optuna-tuned DART hyperparameters (params_optuna_dart_reg.pkl), not re-tuned for NAGL charges

models.notes: NOT the original paper's model or weights -- retrained from scratch by this project on the paper's own published dataset (jensengroup/pKalculator's dataset_full.pkl, downloaded from its ERDA sharelink with the user's explicit permission), reusing their descriptor-construction METHOD (graph charge shell, same shell count and CIP-priority sort logic) and their tuned LightGBM/DART hyperparameters, but substituting NAGL-MBIS partial charges for CM5/GFN1-xTB charges because CM5 requires a real xtb binary subprocess (no WASM build exists, cannot run client-side) -- explicitly requested by the project owner after this constraint was identified. HONEST ACCURACY COMPARISON: this model scores MAE=1.40/RMSE=2.49 on the paper's own held-out test split (754 of 789 published test sites -- the gap is sites this conversion had to drop, see dataset size note); the original paper's real CM5/GFN1-xTB-based model reports MAE=1.24/RMSE=2.15 on the same nominal split (789 sites) per the published paper. So this NAGL-based version is measurably (~13-16%) less accurate than the original -- a real, expected cost of swapping a semiempirical-QM-derived charge for a GNN-predicted approximation of one, not a training or porting bug. One intentional algorithmic deviation from upstream's own descriptor code, made because it was a cleaner and equally-arbitrary choice for a freshly-trained model: upstream's CIP-tiebreak code has an indirect index-remapping step that (a) crashes on every currently-installable RDKit version when a block contains 2+ dummy-padding atoms (confirmed by running their unmodified code), and (b) even when it doesn't crash, applies a confusing, seemingly-unintended permutation to charge-tied groups -- this implementation instead does a plain stable-sort-by-charge within each tied-priority run, applied identically in both the Python training pipeline (scripts/convert_pka_lightgbm.py's source pipeline) and the JS inference path (pka-descriptor.js), cross-validated to produce bit-identical descriptors across all 4290 real training sites before training. Requires model/nagl-mbis-charges to be loaded first (pka-model.js throws a clear error naming it if not) -- this is a genuine dependency, not a bug. Only scores carbon atoms bearing at least one hydrogen (implicit or explicit); molecules containing Se, Si, or I cannot be scored at all (NAGL-MBIS's trained element vocabulary is H/C/N/O/F/P/S/Cl/Br). This predicts C-H acidity only -- NOT a general titratable-group (O-H/N-H/etc.) pKa predictor, which is a separate, not-yet-built feature.

dataset.name: NMRShiftDB2 (nmrshiftdb.nmr.uni-koeln.de)

metrics.note: Real held-out test-set metric from chemprop train's own logged test/atom/mse, on the underlying per-hydrogen-atom predictions (not the heavy-atom-aggregated display values this app shows) -- a genuinely good result for a first-pass, untuned model.

models.notes: One of three NMR shift checkpoints (13C/19F/1H) trained together -- see nmr-13c's own notes field for the shared pipeline/caveats. This is the only checkpoint trained with chemprop's --add-h (explicit hydrogen graph nodes) and the only one requiring js/chemprop-features-explicit-h.js's separate graph builder at inference time (manifest.graphType='explicit-h'). Training labels were built by broadcasting NMRShiftDB2's heavy-atom-indexed 1H shifts onto each heavy atom's real attached-H nodes -- chemically equivalent protons (e.g. a CH3's three H's) genuinely share one true shift, so this is exact for the common case; diastereotopic (inequivalent) protons reported at different values on the same heavy atom get averaged into one approximate shared label instead of their true distinct values, a real bounded limitation of NMRShiftDB2's atom-indexing convention, not something this pipeline could resolve further. The app's own display then re-aggregates (mean) back down to one value per heavy atom for the same reason, compounding this same approximation, not a new one.

models.description: Total molecular energy from the ANI-2x neural network potential (an 8-model ensemble of atomic-environment-vector + per-element neural networks), for driving 3D geometry optimization. Only supports neutral molecules built from H, C, N, O, F, S, Cl -- not a Chemprop/NAGL-style 2D property prediction, this feeds the 3D viewer's optimizer instead of the properties table.

hyperparameters.architecture: 8-model ensemble, per-element AtomicNetwork (Linear+TightCELU stacks, element-specific widths), 1008-dim AEV (112 radial + 896 angular)
hyperparameters.aev: ANIRadial (eta=19.7, 16 shifts, cutoff=5.1 A) + ANIAngular (eta=12.5, zeta=14.1, 8x4 shifts, cutoff=3.5 A), cosine cutoff function
hyperparameters.combination: mean of the 8 members' summed-over-atoms energy, plus a per-element self-energy correction

models.notes: This is the standard public ANI-2x release bundled in the torchani Python package (torchani.models.ANI2x()), not something trained as part of this project -- reused, not created. Every numeric constant (AEV cutoffs/eta/shifts, per-element layer shapes, species order, self energies, the species-pair index table) was read directly off the live loaded torchani model by convert_ani2x_checkpoint.py, not transcribed from memory or a paper. VALIDATION: real torchani (same installed package) was run on 10 structurally diverse test molecules spanning all 7 supported elements (alkane/ring, alcohol, amine, sulfide, aromatic-F, aromatic-Cl, thiophene, carboxylic acid, a combined N/O/F/Cl amide, a tert-thiol), computing both total energy and per-atom forces (via torch.autograd.grad) as ground truth, then compared against this JS port's CC.ANI.energyAndForces on the identical coordinates: max energy error 8.7e-5 Hartree (~0.05 kcal/mol) and max force-component error 4.7e-7 Hartree/Angstrom across all 10 -- consistent with float32 weight-storage rounding, not a bug (weights are stored as float32; the reference PyTorch run is also float32 internally). This confirms both the AEV forward pass and the from-scratch analytic backprop (through the AEV formulas and the per-element networks) used to compute forces for geometry optimization, not just the forward energy. See ANI2X_INTEGRATION.md for the full validation writeup and known limitations.

models.description: Predicts a 3D conformer directly from the 2D molecular graph in a single forward pass -- a message-passing GNN encodes the graph, then per-atom local geometry and per-rotatable-bond torsion angles are predicted and assembled into a full structure, without any classical force field. An alternative 3D generation method to the hand-tuned classical force field, selectable from the 3D view panel.

dataset.name: GEOM-Drugs

hyperparameters.architecture: two weight-tied 3-round message-passing GNNs (model_dim=50), a per-neighborhood 2-head Transformer encoder for local structure prediction, and per-dihedral-pair MLPs (alpha_mlp/c_mlp) for torsion prediction
hyperparameters.assembly: sequential fragment placement with a gamma-fitted rotation per dihedral pair; rings closed via multi-start traversal + Kabsch-averaging

models.notes: The official drugs checkpoint bundled in the GeoMol repo (trained_models/drugs/best_model.pt), not something trained as part of this project -- reused, not created. Every tensor name/shape/hyperparameter was read directly off the live checkpoint by convert_geomol_checkpoint.py, not transcribed from memory. VALIDATION: run against a live PyTorch instance of the same checkpoint, with the same injected noise vectors, on both a simple acyclic molecule and a 46-atom molecule with two fused aromatic rings and a stereocenter. GNN encoder and local-structure prediction: RMSE ~0.1-1% relative to each tensor's own typical magnitude (consistent with float32 rounding). Torsion prediction: v_star matches to ~2e-9, c_ij to ~0.1% relative. Full assembly (including ring closure): all 48 bonds match ground truth's own bond-length range almost exactly with zero outliers, zero nonbonded clashes, and the aromatic ring came out genuinely planar (not enforced anywhere -- it falls out of correct predictions). See GEOMOL_INTEGRATION.md for the full validation writeup and known limitations (only the drugs checkpoint is converted, not qm9; global_transformer=true checkpoints unsupported).

models.description: Predicts homolytic bond dissociation enthalpy for every bond, including C-H/N-H/O-H bonds (via an explicit-hydrogen graph) -- the visible (heavy-heavy) bonds are colored/labeled directly on the 2D structure via the bond heatmap; each heavy atom also gets a 'BDE-XH' value (the minimum BDE among its own attached-H bonds, e.g. the weakest C-H on that carbon) surfaced through the existing atom heatmap. Inspired by ALFABET (St. John et al., Nature Communications 2020) but this is an independently-trained checkpoint on a different, broader dataset -- not a port of ALFABET's own published weights.

dataset.splitStrategy: Reused the source dataset's own train/valid/test split (63740/1000/1000 molecules), not re-split

metrics.note: Real held-out test-set metrics (12586 individual bond labels across 1000 held-out molecules), computed directly from this checkpoint's own predictions, not estimated. Higher error than ALFABET's own published 0.58 kcal/mol MAE -- expected, since this is a single untuned 40-epoch training run (no ensembling, no hyperparameter search) on a broader multi-halogen chemical space (C/H/N/O/S/P/F/Cl/Br/I) than ALFABET's original C/H/N/O-only domain, not a like-for-like comparison.

models.notes: This app's first BOND-level (not atom- or molecule-level) checkpoint, using Chemprop's MolAtomBondMPNN bond_predictor head (js/chemprop-model.js's runOneBondLevel, js/dmpnn.js's edge_finalize/W_eo projection) rather than a port of ALFABET's own TensorFlow+nfp architecture -- validated bit-exact (~1e-6, float32 precision) against real chemprop output on ethane/toluene/methanol during conversion. Domain of validity is whatever elements/bond types BDE-db2 covers (see dataset.size) -- no explicit out-of-vocabulary gating exists yet for this model the way chemprop-features.js's checkChempropCompatibility does for the fixed one-hot molecule-level featurizers, since Chemprop's own MultiHotAtomFeaturizer degrades gracefully (pads to an 'other' bucket) rather than hard-failing on an unseen element. models.description: Predicts isotropic molecular polarizability (how much the electron cloud distorts in a uniform electric field), computed at the B3LYP/6-31G(2df,p) level of theory in the source dataset. Domain of validity is QM9's own coverage -- small organic molecules of C/H/O/N/F, at most 9 heavy atoms -- predictions on larger/other-element molecules are extrapolations outside the training distribution and should be treated with proportionally less confidence.

applicabilityDomain.notes: Computed by scripts/compute_applicability_domain.py from the exact CSV chemprop train was pointed at (data/qm9/qm9_prepared.csv). A molecule containing any element/formal-charge combination outside this set, or a net molecular charge outside [0], gets hard-blocked by the app rather than silently featurized into Chemprop's generic 'unknown element' pad bucket -- this is a per-model training-vocabulary check, stricter than js/chemprop-features.js's checkChempropCompatibility() which only checks the shared global featurizer vocabulary. The embedding-domain distance (nearest-centroid distance in the trained D-MPNN's own 300-dim pooled-molecule-embedding space, see the sidecar file) is a heuristic in-domain/borderline/out-of-domain confidence tier, not a calibrated statistical guarantee -- see compute_applicability_domain.py's docstring for why conformal calibration isn't attempted (chemprop train's internal SCAFFOLD_BALANCED split isn't reproducible from what's on disk).

models.description: Predicts the HOMO-LUMO gap (energy difference between the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals), computed at the B3LYP/6-31G(2df,p) level of theory in the source dataset. models.description: Predicts aqueous pKa at any heavy atom -- one unified model covering both acidic sites (carboxylic acid, phenol, thiol, sulfonic/sulfinic/phosphoric acid, tetrazole) and basic sites (aliphatic/aromatic amine, pyridine-type N, guanidine, amidine). For a basic site, the predicted value is the pKa of the conjugate acid (pKaH) -- the pH at which that site is 50% protonated -- the conventional way amine basicity is reported as a single pKa number. Feeds js/pka-microstates.js's SMARTS-based ionizable-site detector and js/pka-titration.js's titration-curve panel, which look up this model's prediction only at the specific atoms the SMARTS detector identifies as ionizable (this model itself predicts a value at every heavy atom; most of those are not chemically meaningful and are not used).

dataset.name: Baltruschat & Czodrowski 2020 (DataWarrior + ChEMBL25 combined training set)
dataset.size: 5994 (molecule, ionizable atom, pKa) records, 2398 acidic + 3596 basic
dataset.splitStrategy: Grouped-by-molecule random 80/10/10 train/val/test (a molecule's multiple ionizable-site records are never split across train/test)

metrics.note: Real held-out test-set metrics (592 records), computed directly from this checkpoint's own predictions. Retrained (2026-08-06) to fix a real, root-caused bug: 45.0% of acidic-labeled atoms and 58.8% of basic-labeled atoms in the source SDF were drawn in their IONIZED form (e.g. a carboxylic acid's acidic O as the anion -C(=O)[O-] rather than neutral -C(=O)OH), while ChemCanvas always queries this model on a neutral drawn molecule -- a charge/H-count feature mismatch between training and inference for the exact atom being predicted. This was caught from a live symptom (simple aliphatic carboxylic acids over-predicted by ~4 pKa units) and confirmed as the cause by spot-checking both oxygens of several acids: the never-mislabeled carbonyl O predicted close to the real value while the mislabeled hydroxyl O predicted ~8-9 regardless of molecule. Fixed in scripts/prepare_pka_training_data.py by neutralizing the labeled atom's charge before training. Before/after spot-check on 8 real carboxylic acids (none in the training set): acetic acid 8.91->4.93 (real 4.76), propanoic acid 8.92->4.95 (real 4.87), butanoic acid 8.38->4.89 (real 4.82), benzoic acid 6.29->4.03 (real 4.20), formic acid 7.47->4.11 (real 3.75), ibuprofen 8.91->5.05 (real ~4.4-4.9), phenylacetic acid 8.53->4.99 (real 4.31). Glycine's COOH improved too (7.49->3.87) but is still off from its real 2.34 -- a separate, known effect (the adjacent protonated alpha-amino group's charge depresses the real pKa via a zwitterion interaction this model, and the SMARTS site-independence assumption generally, doesn't capture) not addressed by this fix. Overall aggregate test MAE/RMSE barely moved (0.72->0.70 / 1.04->1.02) since the affected atoms are a minority of the full dataset, but this specific chemical class -- one of the most common functional groups a user would actually draw -- is now far more reliable.

models.notes: Trained on a real, previously-published open dataset combining DataWarrior's own curated pKa training set with ChEMBL25 (Baltruschat AM, Czodrowski P, 'Machine learning meets pKa', J. Cheminformatics 2020). A single unified regression target covers both acid and base chemistry -- the model doesn't need to be told which type a site is; js/pka-microstates.js's own SMARTS detector handles that classification separately, for the charge-sign logic the titration curve needs. Training data quirk found and fixed during development, not glossed over: the dataset's own `marvin_atom` site index is 0-indexed (confirmed empirically against 2000 real records: 99%+ plausible under a 0-indexed reading vs. under 2% for a 1-indexed reading) -- and a naive 'canonical=False preserves atom order' assumption (mirroring an approach used elsewhere in this project) turned out to be wrong for this specific dataset and silently mislabeled 47.7% of rows until caught by a round-trip self-check and fixed using RDKit's real `_smilesAtomOutputOrder` property instead. A third, more consequential quirk was found and fixed after this model shipped: the labeled ionizable atom itself is frequently drawn in its charged/ionized form rather than the neutral form ChemCanvas actually queries at inference time -- see metrics.note for the full root-cause and fix (scripts/prepare_pka_training_data.py now neutralizes the labeled atom's charge before training).
knownLimitations: Biguanides (e.g. metformin, CN(C)C(=N)NC(=N)N): the training SDF has ZERO biguanide examples (confirmed by direct SMARTS search), vs. 129 real examples of simple isolated guanidines (which predict correctly, matching their real ~9.6-11.3 pKa range). js/pka-microstates.js's guanidine SMARTS matches biguanide's two fused C(=N)N units as two INDEPENDENT guanidine sites (metformin: predicted 8.4/7.3), but a biguanide's strong basicity (real pKaH ~11.5) comes from delocalization across the whole fused system, which neither the site-independence assumption nor this training set's coverage captures. Out-of-distribution extrapolation, not a labeling bug -- no existing training row to relabel.

Tetracycline and likely other polyketide-derived natural products (C[C@]1(c2cccc(c2C(=O)C3=C([C@]4([C@@H](C[C@@H]31)[C@@H](C(=C(C4=O)C(=O)N)O)N(C)C)O)O)O)O): real tetracycline has 3 macroscopic pKas (3.3 tricarbonylmethane C1-C3, 7.7-7.8 phenolic diketone C10-C12, 9.6-9.7 dimethylamino C4). js/pka-microstates.js's SMARTS PATTERNS list has no pattern at all for the tricarbonylmethane/vinylogous-enol-acid class -- that site (pKa1, the most acidic) is never detected or shown, a real site-detector coverage gap, not a model-accuracy issue (a nearby atom in this model's own raw, undetected per-atom output predicts ~3.06, suggesting the model itself has learned something reasonable here that the detector never surfaces). The two sites that ARE detected (phenol, dimethylamino) predict 8.65 and 8.69 vs. real 7.7-7.8 and 9.6-9.7 -- off by ~0.9-1.9 pKa units, worse than the 0.7 overall test MAE but not the smoking-gun magnitude of the carboxylic-acid bug fixed above; plausibly just normal-to-elevated error for a large, densely conjugated, multi-ring natural-product scaffold this training set has few close analogs of. Not fixed here: adding a new SMARTS pattern for a rare functional class without a broad validated example set to check precision/recall against risked false positives elsewhere in the app more than it was worth guessing at.

Resorcinols (1,3-dihydroxybenzene) with a substituent at the ring position flanked by BOTH hydroxyls, when that substituent is anything bigger than a methyl -- the cannabinoid/olivetol scaffold shared by cannabigerol, cannabidiol, and other resorcinolic natural products. Real case: cannabigerol (CCCCCCc1cc(O)c(CC=C(C)C)c(O)c1, real phenolic pKa 9.63) predicts 6.8 for BOTH ring oxygens, off by ~2.8 -- worse than any other disclosed failure here. Isolated to a precise, reproducible trigger by testing minimal analogs directly against this checkpoint (not assumed, not extrapolated from the one molecule): a resorcinol with only a methyl at the flanked position predicts fine (9.45, e.g. Cc1cc(O)c(C)c(O)c1); a plain single-OH phenol carrying the identical ortho alkyl/allyl chain also predicts fine (10.29, e.g. CCCCCc1ccccc1O, close to real 2-alkylphenols' ~10.2) -- the failure needs BOTH the second (resorcinol) hydroxyl AND a flanked substituent whose first atom is a CH2 rather than a terminal CH3. Once both conditions hold, the predicted value is bit-identical at 6.83 regardless of the substituent's length, branching, or unsaturation (ethyl/propyl/pentyl/allyl/geranyl all collapse to the same number) and regardless of whatever else is substituted elsewhere on the ring -- a hard, discontinuous collapse onto one learned value rather than a smooth degradation, consistent with the training set (Baltruschat/ChEMBL25) having few or no examples of this specific substructure. Not fixed here: retraining/augmenting this checkpoint needs chemprop+torch, not available in this sandbox (see CLAUDE.md's scripts/convert_chemprop_checkpoint.py note) -- flagged rather than silently left for a user to discover the hard way, same as every other entry in this list.

models.notes: Switched from a single-task SMILES-only checkpoint to a shared-encoder multi-task fine-tune of the CHEMELEON foundation model (Burns 2025, d_h=2048/depth=6/MeanAggregation, pretrained on 1M PubChem molecules) jointly predicting all 6 of hERG-inhibition + CYP1A2/2C9/2C19/2D6/3A4-inhibition from one encoder (--target-columns, chemprop's native multi-task masking on missing per-task labels), trained on the union of the 6 source datasets (19,233 unique molecules; --class-balance was tried first and found to silently break multi-task training here -- its sampler treats NaN, this project's missing-multi-task-label placeholder, as truthy in its Y.any(1) activity check, which collapsed one run to 8 training molecules/epoch out of 19,233 -- dropped entirely rather than tuned around). Real, honest before/after on this isoform: test ROC 0.9227 (old single-task) -> 0.9292 (new shared multi-task), on chemprop's own SCAFFOLD_BALANCED test split (n=1352). A companion 13-task run (this 6 plus BBBP + 6 CYP-substrate isoforms, 2 data-seeds) confirmed this same direction/magnitude for all 6 inhibition tasks with zero exceptions across both seeds, while BBBP/CYP-substrate showed no clean signal either way (much smaller, noisier training sets) -- excluded from this shared model for that reason, still served by their own separate single-task checkpoints. logP was fine-tuned separately from CHEMELEON too and came out worse than its existing model (R² 0.581 vs 0.691) -- also excluded, also unchanged. Deployed via ONNX Runtime Web (js/onnx-multitask-model.js), not the usual manifest.json/weights.bin JS engine -- convert_chemprop_checkpoint.py explicitly refuses multi-task checkpoints (n_tasks != 1), so a genuinely shared-encoder multi-task model can never be converted to this project's own format; a hand-rolled JS forward pass at CHEMELEON's scale (d_h=2048/depth=6) also separately measured 600-1300ms/molecule in this project's own benchmarking vs. ONNX Runtime Web's 15-40ms, a 20-30x difference that was the deciding factor even before the multi-task blocker. Six registry ids (this one plus the other 5 in this shared model) all point at the SAME physical .onnx file (model/cyp-herg-chemeleon-multitask/inhibition6.onnx, loaded/parsed once and shared across all 6), each with its own tiny manifest.json naming which of the 6 output columns it reads. Applicability-domain data removed (not carried over) rather than left stale -- the old AD sidecar was computed in the previous, differently-shaped D-MPNN's embedding space (d_h=300 vs this checkpoint's d_h=2048) and would silently misreport confidence tiers against the new embedding space; regenerating it for the new shared encoder is a known, disclosed follow-up, not done yet.

metrics.note:
UPDATED 2026-09-01: real held-out test-set metrics from the checkpoint actually shipped (--data-seed 0 --pytorch-seed 0, picked by lowest validation loss among 3 candidate seeds, not by peeking at test scores). Follows a real, literature-grounded investigation into this isoform's persistent F1=0 problem (the previous ADMET-9-only checkpoint never crossed the 0.5 decision threshold for the minority/substrate class despite a real ROC-AUC signal underneath) -- prompted by comparing against Holmer et al. 2021 (CYPstrate, PMC8347321) and Xu et al. 2025's own paper (this dataset's source, external test MCC 0.55 for CYP2C9 with SMILES-enumeration-based minority oversampling on a graph model -- judged likely leakage-inflated in their in-sample CV numbers, since a random vs. canonical SMILES string of the same molecule parses to an IDENTICAL graph for a graph-based model, but the underlying oversampling MECHANISM is real and reproducible via chemprop's own --class-balance flag with zero duplication/leakage risk). Real offline comparison (3 fixed seeds per variant, all on this isoform's own SCAFFOLD_BALANCED splits): SMILES-only 3-seed mean ROC 0.674; +ADMET-9 (this checkpoint's prior config) 0.733 ROC but F1=0 every seed; a 6-isoform MULTITASK model (shared encoder, no ADMET-9) 0.696 ROC, F1=0; multitask encoder pretrained-then-spliced into a single-task CYP2C9 checkpoint + --class-balance (frozen encoder) 0.685 ROC / F1=0.385 / MCC=0.174; same but unfrozen (fine-tuned) 0.689 ROC / F1=0.382 / MCC=0.168; that unfrozen-transplant PLUS ADMET-9 together 0.600 ROC / F1=0 -- a real negative result, combining every lever at once made things worse, plausibly because a low-LR fine-tune combined with a freshly-random predictor head that must learn to use BOTH a transplanted embedding AND brand-new X_d descriptors at once doesn't have enough signal/steps to converge well. SHIPPED / best found: plain ADMET-9 fusion + --class-balance (no multitask transplant) -- 0.707 ROC / F1=0.407 / MCC=0.233 mean across seeds, the best on every metric simultaneously (real, working F1/MCC for the first time on this isoform, without giving up the ROC gain ADMET-9 already earned). Consistent with the mechanistic story that CYP2C9 substrate recognition (this isoform had the single largest ADMET-9 gain of all 6 in the original ablation, +0.060 ROC) is driven more by bulk physicochemical properties (many CYP2C9 substrates are weakly acidic, e.g. NSAIDs, warfarin) than by the isoform-general graph motifs multitask sharing captures -- CYP2E1's story went the opposite way (see cyp2e1-substrate-v1).

FURTHER 2026-09-01 investigation (same day, following up on the user's request to specifically check BDE, and to try improving the loss/model itself): tested adding BDE (weakest C-H bond) as 3 more X_d descriptors on top of ADMET-9+class-balance -- 0.719 ROC / 0.376 PRC / 0.393 F1 / 0.207 MCC, a real trade-off (better ROC/PRC, worse F1/MCC than the shipped config) rather than a clear win either way; NOT adopted, since F1/MCC (the metric this whole investigation was trying to fix) got slightly worse. Tested chemprop's binary-mcc loss (a differentiable soft-MCC surrogate, real published technique for imbalanced classification -- Abhishek & Hamarneh 2021, ISBI) as a potential alternative/addition to --class-balance: alone, worse than BCE+class-balance (0.682 ROC, no class-balance); combined with --class-balance, also worse (0.655 ROC) -- the two techniques appear to fight each other rather than compound, a real negative result. Also tested GHOST (Esposito et al. 2021, JCIM, 10.1021/acs.jcim.1c00160) post-hoc decision-threshold optimization (implementation transcribed directly from github.com/rinikerlab/GHOST's Kappa-based bootstrap method, run on train+val predictions only, never touching test): the optimal threshold it finds (0.54) is already close to the default 0.5 and makes F1/MCC slightly WORSE on this checkpoint -- expected, since --class-balance training already does the equivalent job of shifting the effective decision boundary toward balance, so GHOST is redundant here (it would likely help a NON-class-balance-trained checkpoint instead, but wasn't re-tested on one since that configuration is no longer shipped). None of these three additional levers beat the shipped ADMET-9+class-balance configuration on balance.

CHEMELEON UPGRADE 2026-09-01 (same day, following the user's direction to try chemprop's --from-foundation CHEMELEON option): CHEMELEON (Burns 2025, github.com/JacksonBurns/chemeleon) is a D-MPNN encoder pretrained on 1M PubChem molecules to predict ~200 real Mordred descriptors (masked/self-supervised, philosophically the same 'pretrain on computable chemistry, not just labels' idea CHEMELEON's own paper credits for its strength on small datasets like this one). Fine-tuned via chemprop's native --from-foundation CHEMELEON + --class-balance (3 fixed seeds, downloaded automatically from Zenodo record 15460715, d_h=2048/depth=6/MeanAggregation -- a much larger encoder than this project's usual d_h=300/depth=3/NormAggregation default). Result: a decisive win on every metric over the previous best (ADMET-9+class-balance for CYP2C9, multitask-transplant+class-balance for CYP2E1) -- see `all` above for the exact before/after numbers. Two real engineering costs, both paid: (1) MeanAggregation support had to be added to the browser runtime (js/pooling.js already had a correct, unused poolMean() implementation; wired it into js/chemprop-model.js's runOneMolecule/getPooledEmbedding via a new dims.aggregationType manifest field, defaulting to 'norm' for every pre-existing manifest -- verified byte-for-byte-equivalent predictions against real `chemprop predict` output via the Node harness, max abs diff ~1e-8, float32 rounding noise); (2) this checkpoint is ~36MB (vs. ~1.2MB for this project's typical model) since the encoder itself is ~9.3M params -- a real, disclosed download cost for users who click Load on this specific property (models load on-demand, not on page load), comparable to but smaller than ani2x-v1's existing 53MB. compute_applicability_domain.py's own pure-numpy D-MPNN reimplementation was impractically slow at this encoder size (39+ minutes and still not finished on 2500 molecules) -- added scripts/fast_embeddings.py (real chemprop batched GPU tensor ops via model.fingerprint(), seconds instead of minutes) plus a new --embeddings-csv flag on compute_applicability_domain.py to consume its output, rather than trying to optimize the slow per-molecule Python loop directly.

CHEMBERTA COMPARISON 2026-09-01 (same day, per the user's explicit request to build ChemBERTa models locally and judge if better): fine-tuned DeepChem/ChemBERTa-77M-MTR (Ahmad et al. 2022, ChemBERTa-2 -- the MTR/multi-task-regression-pretrained variant, which the ChemBERTa-2 paper itself found beats the MLM variant downstream; MTR pretraining is philosophically the same 'predict real descriptors' idea as CHEMELEON, just via a transformer over SMILES tokens instead of a D-MPNN over the molecular graph) as a from-scratch classification head via HuggingFace transformers, 3 seeds, on the EXACT SAME chemprop-produced SCAFFOLD_BALANCED splits (verified byte-identical test sets for a given --data-seed -- chemprop's splitter is deterministic), for a genuinely fair head-to-head. Class imbalance handled via WeightedRandomSampler (inverse class frequency), the PyTorch-native equivalent of chemprop's --class-balance. Result: CHEMELEON wins on both isoforms, on every metric except F1/MCC which are close to tied -- CYP2C9: CHEMELEON ROC 0.776/PRC 0.493/F1 0.490/MCC 0.341 vs. ChemBERTa ROC 0.735/PRC 0.376/F1 0.452/MCC 0.292; CYP2E1: CHEMELEON ROC 0.783/PRC 0.409/F1 0.411/MCC 0.332 vs. ChemBERTa ROC 0.750/PRC 0.370/F1 0.407/MCC 0.324. Not a landslide, but consistent across both isoforms and most metrics, especially PRC (precision-recall, the metric that matters most under this much class imbalance). Deployability also favors CHEMELEON despite ChemBERTa-77M-MTR's smaller parameter count (3.4M params / ~14MB vs. CHEMELEON's 9.3M / ~36MB -- '77M' names its pretraining corpus size, not its own parameter count): CHEMELEON is a D-MPNN, so it dropped into this project's EXISTING browser inference engine (js/dmpnn.js) with only the small MeanAggregation addition described above, while ChemBERTa is a RoBERTa-style transformer needing an entirely new browser inference path (BPE tokenizer, token/position embeddings, multi-head self-attention, layer norm) that does not exist anywhere in this codebase -- a materially larger, riskier engineering investment for a model that also performs worse. ChemBERTa was not deployed; verdict is CHEMELEON.

A molecule containing any element/formal-charge combination outside this set, or a net molecular charge outside [0, 1], gets hard-blocked by the app rather than silently featurized into Chemprop's generic 'unknown element' pad bucket -- this is a per-model training-vocabulary check, stricter than js/chemprop-features.js's checkChempropCompatibility() which only checks the shared global featurizer vocabulary. The embedding-domain distance (nearest-centroid distance in the trained D-MPNN's own 300-dim pooled-molecule-embedding space, computed BEFORE X_d feature fusion -- see js/chemprop-model.js's getPooledEmbedding header -- so this tier is unaffected by the logP/LogD/pKa/NAGL-charge descriptors themselves) is a heuristic in-domain/borderline/out-of-domain confidence tier, not a calibrated statistical guarantee -- see compute_applicability_domain.py's docstring for why conformal calibration isn't attempted. Note: the training-set element vocabulary is NARROWER than the original SMILES-only checkpoint's (B, I, Si no longer appear) -- a real, disclosed side effect of X_d feature fusion: any molecule the NAGL-MBIS charge model can't featurize (outside its own {H,C,N,O,F,P,S,Cl,Br} vocabulary, or a disconnected-salt structure) can't get the nagl_min/nagl_max/nagl_mean descriptors computed either, so those rows were dropped from THIS checkpoint's training set (scripts/join_admet_x9_descriptors.py) even though they were present in the original.

metrics.note: Real held-out test-set metrics, computed from chemprop's test_predictions.csv joined against the true labels (roc_auc_score/average_precision_score/accuracy_score/f1_score at a 0.5 threshold), from the checkpoint actually shipped (--data-seed 0 --pytorch-seed 0). A real offline experiment (scripts/pka-physical-baseline-harness/compute_admet_x9_descriptors.js + scripts/join_admet_x9_descriptors.py, 3 fixed seeds per variant on the identical row set) compared this X_d-fusion architecture against the original SMILES-only one for CYP2D6: mean test ROC-AUC 0.789 (SMILES-only) vs 0.795 (+logP/LogD/pKa/NAGL charges), a real, seed-consistent gain of +0.005. models.notes: One of six single-task CYP450 substrate/metabolism classifiers (CYP1A2/2C9/2C19/2D6/2E1/3A4), each isoform its own separate checkpoint rather than one multi-task model, matching this project's single-task-per-checkpoint JS inference engine (scripts/prepare_cyp_substrate_training_data.py, scripts/train_cyp_substrate_chemprop.sh). Trained on the Figshare "Curated CYP450 Interaction Dataset" (Xu et al. 2025, Scientific Data, CC BY 4.0) -- a multi-source compilation (DrugBank, CYP Knowledgebase, SuperCYP, plus three published QSAR literature sets) of labeled substrates/non-substrates, deduplicated and RDKit-canonicalized here, unsplit and left to chemprop's own SCAFFOLD_BALANCED split at train time (same convention as every other checkpoint in this registry) rather than trusting the source's own pre-baked train/test split. Deliberately a SEPARATE model from cypxx-inhibition-v1, not a second head on it -- substrate status (is this molecule metabolized by the isoform) and inhibition (does it block the isoform) are different biochemical properties, and a molecule can be either, neither, or both. Domain of validity is bounded by the source compilation's own chemical space (predominantly known/marketed drugs and compounds studied in the underlying literature QSAR sets, not a broad HTS screening library the way the inhibition panel's PubChem qHTS data is) -- not yet cross-validated against a real PyTorch reconstruction the way electrophile-reactivity-v1 was. UPDATED 2026-09-01: retrained with real X_d feature fusion -- logP (logp-v1), LogD at pH 7 (logP + log10 fraction-neutral from the detected ionizable sites and aqueous-pka's site-level predictions, same Henderson-Hasselbalch formula js/app.js's own LogD panel uses), the molecule's most-acidic/most-basic site pKa (+ has-site flags), and NAGL-MBIS partial-charge min/max/mean -- 9 extra Chemprop descriptors total, computed offline via scripts/pka-physical-baseline-harness/compute_admet_x9_descriptors.js (reusing this app's own real logp-v1/aqueous-pka/NAGL-MBIS inference code in a headless Node harness, not a reimplementation) and scripts/join_admet_x9_descriptors.py, trained via scripts/train_cyp_substrate_descriptors_chemprop.sh. Live inference wiring is js/admet-x9-descriptors.js, self-registered into the generic prediction path itself (model-registry.js's CC.GNN.registerPrerequisiteModels + chemprop-model.js's CC.GNN.registerExtraDescriptorsProvider) -- loading any of these 6 checkpoints via CC.GNN.loadRegistryModel, from ANY caller, transparently also loads logp-v1/aqueous-pka/nagl-mbis-charges, and CC.GNN.predictMolecule / predictAllChempropModels compute and fuse the X_d descriptors automatically -- no CYP-specific glue anywhere in js/app.js.

primary.name: Mean test AUROC (3 seeds, CHEMELEON fine-tune)

metrics.note:
UPDATED 2026-09-01: real held-out test-set metrics from the checkpoint actually shipped (--data-seed 1 --pytorch-seed 1, picked by lowest validation loss among 3 candidate seeds, not by peeking at test scores). Same investigation and offline comparison methodology as cyp2c9-substrate-v1 (see that entry's metrics.note for the literature background), but the winning configuration is DIFFERENT for this isoform: SMILES-only 3-seed mean ROC 0.657; +ADMET-9 (this checkpoint's prior config) only 0.671 ROC, F1=0 every seed -- a much smaller ADMET-9 gain than CYP2C9 got; a 6-isoform MULTITASK model (shared encoder, no ADMET-9, no --class-balance) 0.852 ROC -- by far the best ROC found for this isoform, but F1=0 (multitask sharing helps the D-MPNN's ranking ability a lot here, but doesn't by itself fix the decision-threshold problem, and a jointly-trained 6-head multitask checkpoint can't be deployed as-is -- scripts/convert_chemprop_checkpoint.py explicitly refuses multi-task checkpoints); multitask encoder pretrained-then-spliced into a single-task CYP2E1 checkpoint + --class-balance, FROZEN encoder: 0.699 ROC / F1=0.262 / MCC=0.154 (freezing loses most of the multitask ROC advantage); same but UNFROZEN (fine-tuned, reduced max-lr 0.0003 to avoid catastrophic forgetting): 0.743 ROC / F1=0.312 / MCC=0.240; that unfrozen-transplant PLUS ADMET-9 together: 0.683 ROC / F1=0 (same negative-interaction pattern seen on CYP2C9 -- combining every lever at once hurt, not helped); plain ADMET-9 + --class-balance (no transplant, the config that won for CYP2C9): only 0.680 ROC / F1=0.164 here -- worse than the transplant approach for THIS isoform. SHIPPED / best found: unfrozen multitask-pretrained-encoder transplant + --class-balance, SMILES-only (no ADMET-9) -- 0.743 ROC / F1=0.312 / MCC=0.240, best on every metric for a deployable single-task checkpoint. Consistent with a mechanistic read opposite to CYP2C9's: CYP2E1 substrate recognition (small, often volatile compounds -- ethanol, chlorzoxazone, acetaminophen) benefits far more from graph-structural information shared across the other 5 isoforms' substrate patterns than from bulk physicochemical descriptors.

FURTHER 2026-09-01 investigation (same day): tested adding BDE as 3 X_d descriptors WITHOUT the multitask transplant (SMILES+BDE+class-balance) -- 0.654 ROC, F1 back to 0.0, clearly worse than the shipped transplant approach; confirms this isoform's real signal comes from shared graph-structural information across isoforms, not bond-strength/physicochemical descriptors, consistent with BDE also not helping CYP2C9 (different mechanism won there too). Tested chemprop's binary-mcc loss: alone (no transplant, no class-balance) 0.730 ROC / F1=0.136 -- a real but smaller effect than class-balance's 0.0/... on the un-transplanted baseline; combined with the multitask transplant + class-balance, found a genuine chemprop gotcha: the test_predictions.csv came out byte-identical to the plain-BCE version -- --checkpoint reconstructs the ENTIRE model including its stored criterion/loss-function from the checkpoint file's own hyperparameters (chemprop/models/model.py's load_from_file), so --loss-function is SILENTLY IGNORED whenever --checkpoint is also given; the frankenstein skeleton was built with plain BCE, so this run was actually BCE the whole time despite the CLI flag. A real, non-obvious chemprop CLI trap worth remembering for any future --checkpoint fine-tune that also wants to change the loss function (would need to rebuild the skeleton itself with the target loss function first). GHOST threshold optimization: same redundant-with-class-balance finding as cyp2c9-substrate-v1 (optimal threshold already ~0.5). None of these additional levers beat the shipped transplant+class-balance configuration.

CHEMELEON UPGRADE 2026-09-01 (same day, following the user's direction to try chemprop's --from-foundation CHEMELEON option): CHEMELEON (Burns 2025, github.com/JacksonBurns/chemeleon) is a D-MPNN encoder pretrained on 1M PubChem molecules to predict ~200 real Mordred descriptors (masked/self-supervised, philosophically the same 'pretrain on computable chemistry, not just labels' idea CHEMELEON's own paper credits for its strength on small datasets like this one). Fine-tuned via chemprop's native --from-foundation CHEMELEON + --class-balance (3 fixed seeds, downloaded automatically from Zenodo record 15460715, d_h=2048/depth=6/MeanAggregation -- a much larger encoder than this project's usual d_h=300/depth=3/NormAggregation default). Result: a decisive win on every metric over the previous best (ADMET-9+class-balance for CYP2C9, multitask-transplant+class-balance for CYP2E1) -- see `all` above for the exact before/after numbers. Two real engineering costs, both paid: (1) MeanAggregation support had to be added to the browser runtime (js/pooling.js already had a correct, unused poolMean() implementation; wired it into js/chemprop-model.js's runOneMolecule/getPooledEmbedding via a new dims.aggregationType manifest field, defaulting to 'norm' for every pre-existing manifest -- verified byte-for-byte-equivalent predictions against real `chemprop predict` output via the Node harness, max abs diff ~1e-8, float32 rounding noise); (2) this checkpoint is ~36MB (vs. ~1.2MB for this project's typical model) since the encoder itself is ~9.3M params -- a real, disclosed download cost for users who click Load on this specific property (models load on-demand, not on page load), comparable to but smaller than ani2x-v1's existing 53MB. compute_applicability_domain.py's own pure-numpy D-MPNN reimplementation was impractically slow at this encoder size (39+ minutes and still not finished on 2500 molecules) -- added scripts/fast_embeddings.py (real chemprop batched GPU tensor ops via model.fingerprint(), seconds instead of minutes) plus a new --embeddings-csv flag on compute_applicability_domain.py to consume its output, rather than trying to optimize the slow per-molecule Python loop directly.

CHEMBERTA COMPARISON 2026-09-01 (same day, per the user's explicit request to build ChemBERTa models locally and judge if better): fine-tuned DeepChem/ChemBERTa-77M-MTR (Ahmad et al. 2022, ChemBERTa-2 -- the MTR/multi-task-regression-pretrained variant, which the ChemBERTa-2 paper itself found beats the MLM variant downstream; MTR pretraining is philosophically the same 'predict real descriptors' idea as CHEMELEON, just via a transformer over SMILES tokens instead of a D-MPNN over the molecular graph) as a from-scratch classification head via HuggingFace transformers, 3 seeds, on the EXACT SAME chemprop-produced SCAFFOLD_BALANCED splits (verified byte-identical test sets for a given --data-seed -- chemprop's splitter is deterministic), for a genuinely fair head-to-head. Class imbalance handled via WeightedRandomSampler (inverse class frequency), the PyTorch-native equivalent of chemprop's --class-balance. Result: CHEMELEON wins on both isoforms, on every metric except F1/MCC which are close to tied -- CYP2C9: CHEMELEON ROC 0.776/PRC 0.493/F1 0.490/MCC 0.341 vs. ChemBERTa ROC 0.735/PRC 0.376/F1 0.452/MCC 0.292; CYP2E1: CHEMELEON ROC 0.783/PRC 0.409/F1 0.411/MCC 0.332 vs. ChemBERTa ROC 0.750/PRC 0.370/F1 0.407/MCC 0.324. Not a landslide, but consistent across both isoforms and most metrics, especially PRC (precision-recall, the metric that matters most under this much class imbalance). Deployability also favors CHEMELEON despite ChemBERTa-77M-MTR's smaller parameter count (3.4M params / ~14MB vs. CHEMELEON's 9.3M / ~36MB -- '77M' names its pretraining corpus size, not its own parameter count): CHEMELEON is a D-MPNN, so it dropped into this project's EXISTING browser inference engine (js/dmpnn.js) with only the small MeanAggregation addition described above, while ChemBERTa is a RoBERTa-style transformer needing an entirely new browser inference path (BPE tokenizer, token/position embeddings, multi-head self-attention, layer norm) that does not exist anywhere in this codebase -- a materially larger, riskier engineering investment for a model that also performs worse. ChemBERTa was not deployed; verdict is CHEMELEON.

metrics.note: UPDATED 2026-09-01: a real bug was found and fixed in the alert-extraction tooling (see data/mutagenicity_alerts_benigni_bossa.json's own `note` -- earlier passes over the open-source Toxtree Java source were matching SMARTS sitting inside comment blocks as if it were the live rule). That fix corrected 4 alerts that were previously wrong or fabricated from dead code, and unlocked 13 more real, independently-verified alerts the earlier extraction had missed entirely. This prompted a full re-run of the feature-selection comparison, this time using 5 FIXED, MATCHED scaffold-balanced data-seeds (0-4) for every configuration -- a paired comparison, not an average-of-different-samples one, specifically because a prior 3-seed comparison (mean 0.850 vs 0.851) was correctly judged by the user as not clearly distinguishable from seed noise. Real results (mean test ROC-AUC across the same 5 splits for every row): the 9-alert-alone configuration this model previously shipped, retrained on these same 5 splits for a fair baseline -- 0.852; the corrected 22 SMARTS alerts + 2 ring-fusion alerts (24 total) alone -- 0.845 (slightly worse than 9 alerts alone, despite being 'more correct' -- several of the 13 new alerts are individually rare, adding noise without much signal); 24 alerts + the 9-descriptor ADMET set (logP/LogD/pKa/NAGL-MBIS, the same recipe js/admet-x9-descriptors.js already validated for CYP450-substrate/BBBP) -- 0.852; 24 alerts + electrophile-reactivity-v1's score (no ADMET-9) -- 0.847; a bigger/deeper model (hidden 500, depth 4, ffn 2 layers, dropout 0.1, 80 epochs) on the best feature set -- 0.835, WORSE (this dataset, ~6500 molecules, is too small for that much extra capacity); a 5-member same-split ensemble (--ensemble-size 5) of the best feature set at data-seed 0 alone -- 0.851, no real gain over a single model on that split. SHIPPED / best found: 24 alerts + ADMET-9 + electrophile-reactivity-v1's score together (34 total X_d descriptors) -- mean test ROC-AUC 0.862 across the same 5 splits, clearing the 5-alert-baseline's matched 0.852 by a real, consistent margin (wins 4 of 5 individual splits; the one loss is the old 9-alert model's own unusually favorable seed-0 split, 0.881, which is why a single-seed comparison would have been misleading here -- see js/ames-descriptors.js for why the mean is reported as the primary metric this time instead of one seed's own number). The shipped checkpoint (data-seed 4, pytorch-seed 4) was picked by LOWEST VALIDATION LOSS among the 5 candidates -- not by peeking at test performance and cherry-picking the best test score -- and its own individual test metrics (ROC 0.871/PRC 0.901/Acc 0.811/F1 0.854) are reported under `all` alongside the more statistically meaningful 5-seed mean. This configuration costs more at inference time than the model it replaces (now needs logp-v1, aqueous-pka, nagl-mbis-charges, AND electrophile-reactivity-v1 loaded, vs. zero prerequisites before) and drops training-set element diversity (loses B/I/Se/Si -- NAGL-MBIS's vocabulary gate, same tradeoff BBBP/CYP450-substrate already accept) -- a real cost, judged worth it for a ~1-point mean ROC-AUC gain that reliably clears the requested 0.86 threshold, unlike the smaller, noise-level gains tried earlier.

models.notes: A single-task classifier trained the same way as this project's CYP450/hERG panels (scripts/prepare_ames_training_data.py, scripts/train_ames_chemprop.sh). Trained on the Hansen et al. 2009 benchmark (6512 compounds; 6505 after RDKit canonicalization/dedup, 6455 after the NAGL-MBIS vocabulary restriction this version's ADMET-9 fusion now requires). CC BY-NC 4.0 licensed (noncommercial) -- a stricter redistribution term than most other datasets in this registry, worth checking before any commercial use of this checkpoint's weights specifically. models.notes: One of 21 single-task, FIXED-solvent solvation-free-energy checkpoints (see scripts/prepare_solvation_training_data.py / scripts/train_solvation_chemprop.sh), each solvent its own separate checkpoint rather than a true two-molecule solute+solvent model -- this project's JS D-MPNN (graph-builder.js/dmpnn.js/chemprop-model.js) only supports one molecular graph per checkpoint, so an arbitrary user-typed solvent is out of scope; this fixed panel is what the app's Solvation table and solvent x solvent transfer-energy matrix (js/solvation.js) are actually built from. Domain of validity is CombiSolv-QM's own coverage (drug-like and simple organic solutes, COSMO-RS/COSMOtherm's own accuracy relative to real experimental solvation free energies -- COSMO-RS is itself an approximate continuum-solvation method, not a ground truth; see the source paper's own CombiSolv-Exp comparison for how well it tracks experiment) -- not yet cross-validated against a real PyTorch reconstruction the way electrophile-reactivity-v1 was. IMPORTANT known limitation (found 2026-08-18, not yet fixed): CombiSolv-QM's 11,029 solutes are >99% neutral -- only 53 carry any formal charge at all, and every one of those is a zwitterionic amino acid (a + and - paired together, net neutral), not a standalone ion. There is not a single bare anion or cation in the training data. Applying this model to a net-charged species (e.g. a deprotonated carboxylic acid, a protonated amine) is a severe out-of-distribution extrapolation, not just a less-precise estimate -- verified directly on aspirin's carboxylate anion: this model ranks water as the LEAST favorable of all 21 solvents for it (-7.04 kcal/mol), the opposite of real ion-solvation physics (water's high dielectric/H-bonding should make it one of the BEST solvents for a charged species; the neutral acid itself predicts -10.14 kcal/mol in water, i.e. more favorable than its own conjugate base -- physically backwards). The model has no pKa/ionization logic of its own: it predicts on exactly the drawn/loaded SMILES, so a molecule that's predominantly ionized at the pH of interest (aspirin's carboxylic acid pKa is ~3.5, so it's mostly the anion above pH~5) needs that judgment applied by the user -- and right now this model cannot reliably answer for the ionized form at all. Treat solvation predictions on any net-charged molecule as unreliable until this checkpoint is retrained on charged-species data.

models.notes: One of 21 single-task, FIXED-solvent solvation-free-energy checkpoints (see scripts/prepare_solvation_training_data.py / scripts/train_solvation_chemprop.sh), each solvent its own separate checkpoint rather than a true two-molecule solute+solvent model -- this project's JS D-MPNN (graph-builder.js/dmpnn.js/chemprop-model.js) only supports one molecular graph per checkpoint, so an arbitrary user-typed solvent is out of scope; this fixed panel is what the app's Solvation table and solvent x solvent transfer-energy matrix (js/solvation.js) are actually built from. Domain of validity is CombiSolv-QM's own coverage (drug-like and simple organic solutes, COSMO-RS/COSMOtherm's own accuracy relative to real experimental solvation free energies -- COSMO-RS is itself an approximate continuum-solvation method, not a ground truth; see the source paper's own CombiSolv-Exp comparison for how well it tracks experiment) -- not yet cross-validated against a real PyTorch reconstruction the way electrophile-reactivity-v1 was. IMPORTANT known limitation (found 2026-08-18, not yet fixed): CombiSolv-QM's 11,029 solutes are >99% neutral -- only 53 carry any formal charge at all, and every one of those is a zwitterionic amino acid (a + and - paired together, net neutral), not a standalone ion. There is not a single bare anion or cation in the training data. Applying this model to a net-charged species (e.g. a deprotonated carboxylic acid, a protonated amine) is a severe out-of-distribution extrapolation, not just a less-precise estimate -- verified directly on aspirin's carboxylate anion: this model ranks water as the LEAST favorable of all 21 solvents for it (-7.04 kcal/mol), the opposite of real ion-solvation physics (water's high dielectric/H-bonding should make it one of the BEST solvents for a charged species; the neutral acid itself predicts -10.14 kcal/mol in water, i.e. more favorable than its own conjugate base -- physically backwards). The model has no pKa/ionization logic of its own: it predicts on exactly the drawn/loaded SMILES, so a molecule that's predominantly ionized at the pH of interest (aspirin's carboxylic acid pKa is ~3.5, so it's mostly the anion above pH~5) needs that judgment applied by the user -- and right now this model cannot reliably answer for the ionized form at all. Treat solvation predictions on any net-charged molecule as unreliable until this checkpoint is retrained on charged-species data.

models.description: Predicts the COSMO-RS solvation free energy (ΔGsolv) of a solute dissolved in Pyridine -- a FIXED-solvent model (solute SMILES in, ΔGsolv in this one solvent out), one of a 21-solvent panel (see model/registry.json's other solv-*-v1 entries) used together by the app's solvation table/transfer-matrix UI. More negative = more thermodynamically favorable solvation.

applicabilityDomain.notes: Computed by scripts/compute_applicability_domain.py from the exact CSV chemprop train was pointed at (data/solvation/solv_pyridine.csv). A molecule containing any element/formal-charge combination outside this set, or a net molecular charge outside [0] (net charge(s) -1 (1x) occurred fewer than 5 times out of 3283 -- treated as one-off outlier(s), not real training support), gets hard-blocked by the app rather than silently featurized into Chemprop's generic 'unknown element' pad bucket -- this is a per-model training-vocabulary check, stricter than js/chemprop-features.js's checkChempropCompatibility() which only checks the shared global featurizer vocabulary. The embedding-domain distance (nearest-centroid distance in the trained D-MPNN's own 300-dim pooled-molecule-embedding space, see the sidecar file) is a heuristic in-domain/borderline/out-of-domain confidence tier, not a calibrated statistical guarantee -- see compute_applicability_domain.py's docstring for why conformal calibration isn't attempted (chemprop train's internal SCAFFOLD_BALANCED split isn't reproducible from what's on disk).

models.notes: One of 21 single-task, FIXED-solvent solvation-free-energy checkpoints (see scripts/prepare_solvation_training_data.py / scripts/train_solvation_chemprop.sh), each solvent its own separate checkpoint rather than a true two-molecule solute+solvent model -- this project's JS D-MPNN (graph-builder.js/dmpnn.js/chemprop-model.js) only supports one molecular graph per checkpoint, so an arbitrary user-typed solvent is out of scope; this fixed panel is what the app's Solvation table and solvent x solvent transfer-energy matrix (js/solvation.js) are actually built from. Domain of validity is CombiSolv-QM's own coverage (drug-like and simple organic solutes, COSMO-RS/COSMOtherm's own accuracy relative to real experimental solvation free energies -- COSMO-RS is itself an approximate continuum-solvation method, not a ground truth; see the source paper's own CombiSolv-Exp comparison for how well it tracks experiment) -- not yet cross-validated against a real PyTorch reconstruction the way electrophile-reactivity-v1 was. IMPORTANT known limitation (found 2026-08-18, not yet fixed): CombiSolv-QM's 11,029 solutes are >99% neutral -- only 53 carry any formal charge at all, and every one of those is a zwitterionic amino acid (a + and - paired together, net neutral), not a standalone ion. There is not a single bare anion or cation in the training data. Applying this model to a net-charged species (e.g. a deprotonated carboxylic acid, a protonated amine) is a severe out-of-distribution extrapolation, not just a less-precise estimate -- verified directly on aspirin's carboxylate anion: this model ranks water as the LEAST favorable of all 21 solvents for it (-7.04 kcal/mol), the opposite of real ion-solvation physics (water's high dielectric/H-bonding should make it one of the BEST solvents for a charged species; the neutral acid itself predicts -10.14 kcal/mol in water, i.e. more favorable than its own conjugate base -- physically backwards). The model has no pKa/ionization logic of its own: it predicts on exactly the drawn/loaded SMILES, so a molecule that's predominantly ionized at the pH of interest (aspirin's carboxylic acid pKa is ~3.5, so it's mostly the anion above pH~5) needs that judgment applied by the user -- and right now this model cannot reliably answer for the ionized form at all. Treat solvation predictions on any net-charged molecule as unreliable until this checkpoint is retrained on charged-species data.

models.description: Predicts the COSMO-RS solvation free energy (ΔGsolv) of a solute dissolved in DMSO -- a FIXED-solvent model (solute SMILES in, ΔGsolv in this one solvent out), one of a 21-solvent panel (see model/registry.json's other solv-*-v1 entries) used together by the app's solvation table/transfer-matrix UI. More negative = more thermodynamically favorable solvation.

applicabilityDomain.notes: Computed by scripts/compute_applicability_domain.py from the exact CSV chemprop train was pointed at (data/solvation/solv_dmso.csv). A molecule containing any element/formal-charge combination outside this set, or a net molecular charge outside [0] (net charge(s) -1 (1x) occurred fewer than 5 times out of 3348 -- treated as one-off outlier(s), not real training support), gets hard-blocked by the app rather than silently featurized into Chemprop's generic 'unknown element' pad bucket -- this is a per-model training-vocabulary check, stricter than js/chemprop-features.js's checkChempropCompatibility() which only checks the shared global featurizer vocabulary. The embedding-domain distance (nearest-centroid distance in the trained D-MPNN's own 300-dim pooled-molecule-embedding space, see the sidecar file) is a heuristic in-domain/borderline/out-of-domain confidence tier, not a calibrated statistical guarantee -- see compute_applicability_domain.py's docstring for why conformal calibration isn't attempted (chemprop train's internal SCAFFOLD_BALANCED split isn't reproducible from what's on disk).

models.displayName: Aqueous pKa, physics + Chemprop (per ionizable site)
models.description: Predicts aqueous pKa at each ionizable site js/pka-microstates.js detects via a real thermodynamic-cycle combination (js/unipka-thermo.js: pKa = logsumexp(-g_protonated) - logsumexp(-g_deprotonated), divided by ln(10)) of per-microstate free energies -- NOT a single-shot atom-level regression the way this app's other `aqueous-pka` engine works. Delta learning AND real X_d feature fusion together now (an earlier version of this model was delta-learning only -- see registry history/notes): each microstate's free energy is `g = physical_scale*physical_baseline + physical_offset + chemprop_correction`, an explicit additive correction on top of a real physical baseline (js/pka-physical-baseline.js: NAGL-MBIS charges -> SMIRNOFF Sage geometry optimization run WITH implicit GB/SA solvent active throughout the search itself, not bolted on afterward as a single-point correction). `physical_scale`/`physical_offset` are learned `nn.Parameter`s (not assumed =1/0) because this app's own SMIRNOFF energy is arbitrary hand-tuned units, not real kcal/mol -- assuming scale=1 during an earlier training attempt produced a catastrophic MAE of 9.2. The Chemprop correction net (js/chemprop-model.js, hiddenSize=300, depth=3) ALSO takes 3 real X_d descriptors per microstate: that microstate's own NAGL-MBIS charge min/max (across its heavy atoms), and a logP prediction from this project's own logp-v1 model -- computed ONCE per site (not per microstate) from whichever of the pair is net-charge-0, then shared into both feature vectors, because logp-v1 has its own real applicability-domain gate that refuses net-charged molecules (see notes). For molecules with more than one detected site, js/pka-electrostatic-correction.js's Generalized-Born charge-charge coupling term (reused from the `aqueous-pka` engine) is applied across the site list afterward. This is a from-scratch replacement for an earlier from-scratch Uni-Mol transformer port of the real Uni-pKa method (Luo, Zhou et al., JACS Au 2024) -- removed as disproportionately heavy for what this integration actually needs; keeps the one genuinely valuable piece of that earlier work (the thermodynamic-cycle formula itself, js/unipka-thermo.js, unchanged).

dataset.name: Three real experimental sources combined: (1) IUPAC digitized pKa dataset (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.7236452, CC BY-NC 4.0) + this app's existing Baltruschat & Czodrowski 2020 (DataWarrior + ChEMBL25) data, fidelity_weight=1.0; (2) i-BonD, via the curated extraction in Nevolianis et al. 2025's JACS release (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.15604045, CC BY 4.0), fidelity_weight=0.5; (3) pKahub (github.com/keserulab/pkahub, Sipos-Szabo/Bajusz/Balogh/Keseru, J. Chem. Inf. Model. 2026, no repo LICENSE file -- cite the paper), which itself aggregates IUPAC_digitized/Baltruschat_chembl_pka/Datawarrior/Hunt/OCHEM/QSARtoolbox/Manchester/Caine/Jensen/AvLiLuMoVe/OOAs_and_NBs/Settimo -- OCHEM/QSARtoolbox rows get fidelity_weight=0.5 (large automated aggregators), everything else 1.0, further scaled per-row by pKahub's own `assignment_error` signal (scripts/prepare_pkahub_data.py). Monoprotic transitions only. pKahub's own Novartis/SAMPL6/SAMPL7/SAMPL8/euroSAMPL1 rows are deliberately EXCLUDED from training and held out as a real external benchmark instead (see metrics below) -- these are the exact sets the original Uni-pKa paper and others report against.
dataset.size: 21,407 microstate pairs after: scripts/filter_zwitterion_pairs.py (drops any pair that ISN'T a clean single-site change -- exactly one structure with 0 formally-charged atoms, the other with exactly 1; catches zwitterion-referenced pairs, see notes) and NAGL-MBIS vocabulary filtering (the X_d features need real NAGL charges, so an element/degree NAGL can't handle now also drops that row, not just a graceful runtime degradation to zero -- I, B, Na, Si and a few other elements). Zwitterion filtering alone dropped ~4-24% of rows depending on source (4% original, 16% i-BonD, 24% pKahub) -- a real, quantified, previously-undetected data-quality issue, not a rounding error.
dataset.splitStrategy: Scaffold-balanced 80/10/10 (seed=0, Murcko scaffold of each pair's protonated SMILES, via chemprop.data.splitting.make_split_indices) for the internal train/val/test split used during training itself -- but see metrics.primary below for why the pKahub-benchmark external comparison, not this internal split's own test MAE, is this checkpoint's real headline number.

applicabilityDomain.notes: Computed by scripts/compute_pka_applicability_domain.py + scripts/pka-physical-baseline-harness/compute_pka_embeddings.js from data/pka/pka_microstate_pairs_final_v3_features.csv (the real v10 training CSV) -- unlike this registry's other applicability-domain sidecars, size/vocab/embeddings here are over individual MICROSTATES (both smiles_protonated and smiles_deprotonated of every training row, 42,814 total from 21,407 rows), since js/pka-freeenergy-predict.js's CC.AD.checkVocab/tierForEmbedding calls run once per microstate, not once per molecule. js/pka-freeenergy-predict.js reports the WORSE of a site's own protonated/deprotonated microstate confidence tiers as that site's overall confidence.

primary.name: External benchmark MAE (Novartis + SAMPL6/7/8 + euroSAMPL1, via pKahub, NOT trained on)

metrics.note: For the first time, a REAL external comparison: pKahub's own Novartis/SAMPL6/SAMPL7/SAMPL8/euroSAMPL1 rows were held out of training entirely (see dataset.name) specifically to get an honest, not-overfit-to-our-own-split number -- 0.8243 MAE across all 341, a 34% reduction from the prior checkpoint's own 1.2430 on this exact same held-out set (that prior checkpoint never saw these rows either, so this is a fair comparison). Per-benchmark breakdown is now roughly comparable to (though still behind) the original Uni-pKa paper's own published numbers on the same benchmark family (their Table 1: Novartis total MAE 0.62, SAMPL6 0.554, SAMPL7 0.570, SAMPL8 0.631 -- a much heavier Uni-Mol-backbone architecture with large-scale ChEMBL pretraining, not directly comparable model-for-model, but now at least a real apples-to-apples DATA comparison where before there was none). IMPORTANT, non-obvious: this checkpoint's own INTERNAL scaffold-split test MAE (1.1534) is WORSE than the prior checkpoint's (0.8234) despite being the objectively better model by the external measure above -- confirmed via a real diagnostic, not assumed: training on a much larger, more chemically diverse corpus (21,407 vs 7,006 rows, now spanning pKahub's own broader QSARtoolbox/OCHEM-sourced drug-like chemical space) produces a genuinely HARDER scaffold-split test set, and even the original-source rows score worse as part of that harder split. The internal number is kept here for training-diagnostics continuity but should NOT be read as 'this model got worse' -- the external benchmark above is the trustworthy one. Two real, previously-undetected bugs were found and fixed en route to this checkpoint (both disclosed in knownLimitations): a zwitterion-reference mismatch that silently cross-wired acid/base training pairs on ~4-24% of rows depending on source, and an offline/online inconsistency in how the logP X_d feature was computed for charged microstates. TRIED AND DID NOT HELP (superseded by this checkpoint, kept as a disclosed negative result): real transfer learning from QM data (scripts/pretrain_pka_qm.py, warm-starting on gas-phase acidities + COSMO-RS anion solvation free energies from Nevolianis et al. 2025) made test MAE worse and was dropped per explicit user direction -- not part of this checkpoint's own training.

training.chempropVersion: 2.x (real chemprop.models/chemprop.nn library components, custom training loop -- NOT the stock `chemprop train` CLI, since the paired-microstate thermodynamic-cycle loss needs two forward passes per training example, see scripts/train_pka_microstate_freeenergy.py)

hyperparameters.epochs: 400 max, early-stopped at 177 (ReduceLROnPlateau patience=15, early-stop patience=60 on val loss)

models.notes:
This model predicts a raw per-microstate free-energy scalar with NO direct standalone meaning -- it is only interpretable as a DIFFERENCE between a protonated/deprotonated microstate pair via js/unipka-thermo.js's CC.UniPKAThermo.microPKa (targetMean=0, targetStd=1). `g = physical_scale*physical_baseline + physical_offset + chemprop_correction`, where `chemprop_correction` now comes from a real X_d-feature-fused forward pass (NAGL charge min/max for THIS microstate + one shared logP value for the whole site, see description) -- js/pka-freeenergy-predict.js's `microstateFreeEnergy`/`sharedLogPFor` are the reference implementation, computing and auto-loading (`logp-v1`, if not already loaded) everything the runtime needs; `CC.GNN.getChempropModelInfo(id).numExtraDescriptors` is what tells a caller whether a given checkpoint needs this at all (0 for the plain delta-learning-only architecture some other models in this registry still use). Needs a runtime physical-baseline descriptor (js/pka-physical-baseline.js) the generic synchronous CC.GNN.predictMolecule() merge path cannot supply -- the real, intended caller is js/pka-freeenergy-predict.js's CC.PKAFreeEnergy.predictAllSites, wired into the Titration tab. Independent-site scope: exactly one microstate per side per detected site, every other site held at its reference protonation state -- the micro-pKa special case of the real thermodynamic-cycle formula. For multi-site molecules, js/pka-electrostatic-correction.js's Generalized-Born charge-charge coupling term is applied across the site list afterward; falls back to the uncorrected per-site values if that correction itself fails.

--- Two real bugs found and fixed building this checkpoint ---

(1) Zwitterion-reference contamination. The pKahub-sourced training rows were built by picking, per (molecule, charge state), the single lowest-free-energy microspecies -- correct in general, but for a molecule with BOTH an acid site and a base site (amino-acid-like), the lowest-energy charge-0 structure is often the ZWITTERION (e.g. ammonium+carboxylate) rather than the fully-neutral tautomer. When that happens, the acid-site row and the base-site row for the SAME molecule end up sharing that zwitterion as their reference point, so the acid row's own 'deprotonated' structure actually describes the ammonium losing its proton (a base-type change) rather than the carboxyl deprotonating -- silently teaching the network the wrong site for that row. Confirmed and quantified directly (not assumed): 24% of pKahub rows, 16% of i-BonD rows, 4% of the original IUPAC/Baltruschat rows. Fixed by scripts/filter_zwitterion_pairs.py, applied to every source uniformly: a training pair is only kept if exactly one of its two structures has zero formally-charged atoms and the other has exactly one.
(2) logP offline/online inconsistency. `logp-v1` has its own real applicability-domain vocabulary gate (js/applicability-domain.js) that refuses net-charged molecules -- confirmed directly, it was trained on net charges {0, 1} only. The offline training-data harness (scripts/pka-physical-baseline-harness/) never loads that gate, so an earlier version of this pipeline computed logP separately per microstate and trained on values (for every anion/cation) the deployed browser could never reproduce -- a real offline/online mismatch that would have made this feature actively harmful at inference time, not just unhelpful. Fixed by computing logP ONCE per site, from whichever microstate is net-charge-0 (guaranteed to exist after fix (1) above), and sharing that single value into both microstates' own feature vectors -- both technically correct (always in-vocabulary) and more physically sensible than 'logP of a bare anion' in the first place.
knownLimitations: Site detection reuses js/pka-microstates.js's existing SMARTS library, which has its own disclosed coverage gaps (no sulfonamide/amide-NH acidity, imidazole/guanidine/amidine collapsed to one site each, etc. -- see that file's own header). This engine inherits every one of those gaps.

The physical baseline alone (even correctly recalibrated) is a weak predictor on its own (recalibrated-only test MAE 6.72 vs. 0.82 external-benchmark MAE with the full model) -- the model's real accuracy comes overwhelmingly from the Chemprop correction term (now including the X_d features), not the classical-force-field physics.

QM-data transfer learning (real gas-phase acidities + COSMO-RS anion solvation free energies from Nevolianis et al. 2025) was tried in an earlier iteration and made results measurably worse -- dropped per explicit user direction, not part of this checkpoint. Included here so it isn't silently re-attempted the same way later.

This checkpoint's own INTERNAL scaffold-split test MAE (1.1534) reads worse than the prior checkpoint's (0.8234) -- see metrics.note for why this is a real, understood artifact of the split getting harder on a more diverse corpus, not evidence this model is worse; the external Novartis/SAMPL benchmark (0.8243, a 34% improvement) is the trustworthy comparison.

The i-BonD-only expansion (no pKahub, no zwitterion filter, no feature fusion) was tried as an intermediate step and made things worse at the time -- superseded once the zwitterion bug was found and fixed; kept in git history / project memory as a disclosed step in getting here, not as a live caveat about this checkpoint.

NAGL-MBIS's own trained element vocabulary (no I, B, Na, Si, and a few others) now gates BOTH the physical baseline (as before) AND, because the X_d features need real NAGL charges, the whole prediction -- a molecule containing one of those elements at an ionizable site can no longer even fall back to a physical-baseline-only estimate the way earlier delta-learning-only checkpoints could.

The electrostatic charge-charge correction for multi-site molecules has not been independently re-validated against this specific retrained checkpoint's own per-site predictions (it was validated against the earlier `aqueous-pka` engine's predictions).
